items.title: Stars Who Have Broken Grammy Records: Beyonce, Taylor Swift and More
items.summary:
Beyoncé and Taylor Swift are just a few of the big names who have broken Grammy records over the course of the awards show’s history.

In 2023, Beyoncé became the most-awarded artist in Grammys history with the 32nd trophy of her career, taking home the trophy for Best Dance/Electronic Album for Renaissance . It was her fourth win of the 2023 ceremony.

Two years later, Beyoncé added even more Grammy wins to her resume thanks to Cowboy Carter, becoming the first Black woman to win Best Country Album. She also won Album of the Year and Best Country/Duo Group Performance for “II Most Wanted” with Miley Cyrus .

Another Grammys favorite, Billie Eilish , swept the 2020 awards show with wins in the biggest categories of the night, including Album of the Year, Song of the Year, Record of the Year and Best New Artist, when she was just 18 years old.

“[Billie] was very grateful, obviously, and a lot of her friends were there,” her brother, Finneas O’Connell , told Vogue in February 2020. “She has more ‘go with the flow’ than I do, but we were both kind of embarrassed to win so much; you hope that it will be kind of equal, but after the third in a row … Well, we love all our fellow nominees.”

The producer noted that he was pulling for Lizzo or Lil Nas X . “If I’d bet on anyone, I would have lost money in us winning everything,” he said.

items.summary:
Peacock’s The Good Daughter kept viewers guessing its entire first season — but could the show return for more episodes?

Based on Karin Slaughter ‘s book of the same name, The Good Daughter picks up 20 years after a violent attack on a family — with sisters Charlotte ( Meghann Fahy ) and Samantha Quinn ( Rose Byrne ) still living with the trauma. Charlotte, who has followed her father into the legal field, is the first witness on the scene when another brutal attack takes place in their hometown, and ultimately the investigation brings back old memories and family secrets.

In addition to Byrne, 47, and Fahy, 36, the show stars Brendan Gleeson, Harper Steele, Paula Malcomson, Jake McDorman, Olivia Williams and Michael Dorman . Despite there only being one book in the series, executive producers Bruna Papandrea and Steph Green addressed the show’s future beyond season 1.

“I just don’t think when we do anything now. If you’d asked me when we made Big Little Lies if there would be more, I would have said no. It’s like you’ll never get this group of people together again. It was a one-off, right? Cut to where we are now,” Papandrea exclusively told Us, referencing the HBO series developing its third season. “This was definitely built as a limited series, that’s for sure. items.title: Stars Who Have Played James Bond Over the Years
items.summary:
James Bond is one of the most iconic characters in cinematic history — and yet, only a handful of actors have been fortunate enough to tackle the part.

The popular action film franchise is based on a character created by author Ian Fleming for his James Bond book series . EON Productions gained the rights to distribute all related movies in 1962, beginning with Dr. No .

Pierce Brosnan , Timothy Dalton and Roger Moore are among those who have served as the British spy. However, Sean Connery has often been regarded as the best actor to step into the role.

When he died in October 2020 of respiratory failure, fellow Bond actor Daniel Craig praised Connery for the way he “defined an era and a style” with his take on the character.

“The wit and charm he portrayed onscreen could be measured in megawatts; he helped create the modern blockbuster,” the Logan Lucky actor said in a statement on the official 007 website . “He will continue to influence actors and filmmakers alike for years to come.”

Craig, for his part, took his fifth and final leap as Bond in 2021’s No Time to Die after 15 years in the role. In November 2026, Robert Pattinson was officially cast as the new 007.

items.summary:
Daris Rucker is opening up about the highs and lows of his life in the spotlight.

“For a lot of years, I experienced some real low lows,” Rucker, 60, shared in his new Hulu documentary Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie . “One of the hardest parts of my life is getting divorced.”

The country singer and ex Beth Leonard announced in July 2020 that they had split after 20 years of marriage . During their relationship, the pair welcomed daughter Daniela in 2001 and son Jack in 2004. (Rucker and his ex Elizabeth Ann Phillips also welcomed daughter Carolyn in 1995.)

“Beth and I stayed together for a lot of years after I stopped partying,” Rucker shared in a new interview featured in the documentary. “I just think we had gotten to a point where the growing apart thing sounds so cliché, but that’s really what it is. It was an awful time.”

Tim McGraw, Faith Hill and More of Country Music’s Biggest Couples 

The former Hootie and the Blowfish frontman added, “Divorce is awful. It was an awful time, and I look at it as another chapter of life that’s closed.”

In the documentary, old quotes from Rucker appeared on the screen where he discussed the end of his marriage.

“My ex-wife did everything to make my life great,” he once said, “and I did everything in my power to mess it up.”

Although he’s been able to receive a second chance of love by getting engaged to singer Emily Deahl , Rucker still can’t help but feel sentimental when looking back on that admittedly painful chapter of his life.

“I tried to come out of it as a better person and a better dad,” he said in the doc.…

Aaron Rodgers didn’t appreciate the line of questioning from ESPN reporter Brooke Pryor following the Pittsburgh Steelers’ blowout loss at the hands of the Cincinnati Bengals on Sunday, November 15.  

During a post-game press conference after the 36-18 defeat, Pryor asked Rodgers, “How do you keep a loss like this from changing the trajectory of your season?” 

“That’s very dramatic there, Brooke,” the quarterback, 42, said with a smile. Rodgers continued, “You know, I’ve been a part of this league for a long time. There’s big wins, there’s tough losses. We’ll deal with this appropriately.” 

Pryor asked Rodgers a follow-up question about the team’s road struggles this season — they are 2-3 away from home, while a perfect 4-0 in Pittsburgh — but he was similarly disinterested.

“Yeah, I don’t know,” he said. “We’ll look at that.” 

Pryor, who has worked for ESPN since 2019, managed to have some fun with the viral interaction. She posted a clip from Rodgers’ answer via Instagram , writing, “Am I the drama?” 

Rodgers and the Steelers started remarkably slow on Sunday night, with the quarterback racking up only 27 passing yards through the first three quarters. He finished 15-for-29 passing for 143 yards and two touchdowns.  

After the game, Rodgers said he was “not happy with the way we performed on offense.” 

“Couldn’t get anything going until the fourth quarter,” he continued. “So that’s disappointing.” 

Rodgers added, “We kind of shot ourselves in the foot with a couple plays.”

items.title: I saw how brightly stars like Russell Brand could shine, but there is darkness in the shadows | Sophie Heawood
items.summary:
After years of celebrity interviews, I have learned not to be fooled by the allure of fame. We never really know them – we know what they want us to know

As I sat in Southwark crown court, listening to the final day of Russell Brand’s trial, there was one subject that came up repeatedly, invoked as often by his defence as the prosecution. I don’t mean sex or coercion, but fame. It ran through every victim impact statement and loomed so large in the courtroom that it felt as if it was almost on trial itself.

I’m an entertainment journalist who has been covering celebrities for more than 20 years – as long as Brand has been one – and I have written about him at various stages of his career. But I went to Southwark crown court as a member of the public who wanted to see justice done. For the women he had hurt, for the ones who couldn’t get as far as the courtroom, and for all of us who came of age at a time when rape culture was so fast and furious that young women mistook it for a joke that we were in on. In the age of lads’ mags, sex felt cheapened, yet somehow we were the ones who ended up paying for this. So it was doubly strange to sit in court and feel somehow complicit in it - in how this media culture had encouraged Russell Brand.

Continue reading...
items.t: I saw how brightly stars like Russell Brand could shine, but there is darkness in the shadows | Sophie Heawood

items.title: Two courtrooms, one celebrity: how did the Russell Brand case compare with the rape trial next door?
items.summary:
One was a high-profile defendant watched by more than 100 journalists. Another was an unknown man who preyed on a girl almost half his age. Their stories played out minutes apart, one entirely out of the spotlight

What is going on inside Russell Brand’s head as he arrives at court for the start of his rape trial? He sees the dozens of cameras and journalists lined outside Southwark crown court, many of whom have been waiting since before 7am, and he tells himself that the media are all against him. “It seems to me that they believe that I am guilty, and that this should be the rubber-stamping of the process of my destruction.”

He walks with his wife, Laura, and his bodyguard past the photographers, “clickering, clackering, snickering paparazzi, like locusts, peculiar concoctions, not fully humans”, and up into the court, where he is suddenly overwhelmed by “the presence of something very beautiful, grace”. “In a situation like I’m in, it’s impossible not to turn to God. Truth and justice are the only things that can save me,” he thinks.

items.t: Two courtrooms, one celebrity: how did the Russell Brand case compare with the rape trial next door?
